A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SU(2)-based rotation-estimation work. All pages, including appendices, are readable, and methods, proofs, figures, and retained results can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic Wahba simulations, neural-network learning experiments, NeRF camera-orientation experiments, and timing measurements in Section 5 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v3 retains original synthetic results and reports additional object-orientation, inverse-kinematics, camera-pose, and representation-analysis experiments in Section 5 and Appendices F–G.

M1.justification: The Wahba solvers, exact-alignment procedures, 2-vec, and QuadMobius mappings are retained. v3 Eq. (26) algebraically combines the normalizations in v1 Eq. (48). The new residual and axis-prior passages describe applications of existing constraints without establishing a changed core estimator.

E1.justification: v3 removes the NeRF synthetic lego experiment and adds object orientation from ModelNet10-SO3 images, inverse kinematics using human motion-capture poses, and joint camera-pose prediction on Cambridge Landmarks. Appendix F also introduces dropout-corrupted and outlier-contaminated input scenarios. Synthetic Wahba coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The established solver and learning baseline sets remain; Fast Quat is renamed Fast 2 Vec, still citing Markley (2002). Appendix F adds projection-only and eigendecomposition-only comparisons in Table 3 and a qualitative comparison with direct SU(2) prediction. Extending existing baselines to new benchmarks does not itself change their membership.

E3.justification: New protocols include ModelNet angular-accuracy thresholds and category-specific training budgets, joint-position losses for inverse kinematics, and joint rotation/translation training with checkpoint selection for camera pose. Appendix F specifies 1,000-input diagnostic studies and a 10,000-input component study. The retained synthetic experiments preserve their original generation and training design.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds gradient-balance analysis for 2-vec versus Gram-Schmidt, dropout sensitivity at different QuadMobius stages, gradient analysis under 10% outlier contamination, and component ablations separating projection and eigendecomposition. These investigate mechanisms and robustness beyond the retained noise-level and learning-configuration comparisons.

E5.justification: Two-point solver reporting expands from median error alone in v1 Table 2 to 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles in v3 Table 5, adding empirical dispersion summaries. The million-trial and 10,000-timing-measurement counts remain unchanged. Neither version reports confidence intervals or uncertainty across repeated training seeds.

E6.justification: v3 adds benchmark and diagnostic results while removing the NeRF results. For example, its new King's College comparison reports mean angular errors of 2.631 degrees for QMAlg and 3.204 for QCQP. General Wahba results, all 24 learning configurations, and representation timings remain numerically unchanged. Two-point tail percentiles are newly reported; these changes do not establish same-setting performance gains between versions.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds derivations of 2-vec and both QuadMobius mapping formulas. Appendix B.3.2 derives the polar-factor derivative through a Sylvester equation, whereas v1 explicitly omitted that derivation. The original metric, nearest-unitary, and two-point solution proofs are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract and new Contributions subsection broaden the stated application scope from minimal closed-form Wahba cases to related rotation-optimization problems, illustrated by residual and axis-prior uses in Sections 3.1–3.2. The central SU(2) derivations and two learning representations remain the principal contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds explanations linking 2-vec to balanced gradients and QuadMobius to a stable intermediate representation followed by predictable projection gradients. It also discusses double-cover and redundancy problems in direct SU(2) prediction. Removing the NeRF experiment removes its specific overfitting interpretation; existing singularity and computational-cost qualifications largely remain.

D1.justification: Appendix G.1 supplies architectures, pretraining, dropout, training budgets, batch sizes, camera-loss weights, hardware, and checkpoint-selection details for the new benchmarks. G.2.2 newly identifies the retained synthetic network's source and T4 hardware, without establishing a hardware change or rerun. B.3.2 documents zero-division handling. NeRF implementation details disappear with that experiment.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting axis-prior applications and new evaluation tasks, including Chandrasekhar, Magner and Zee, Chen, Kendall, Liao, and Walch, while removing the NeRF reference. Positioning relative to Gram-Schmidt, SVD, QCQP, and classical Wahba solvers remains substantially intact.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: mathematical background moves to Appendix A, rotation recovery to C.1, exact-alignment procedures to D, and synthetic learning experiments to G.2.2. A Contributions subsection and rewritten Sections 3 and 5 foreground applications and learning benchmarks. Derivation explanations are also substantially expanded.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. v3 adds a conceptual diagram, benchmark tables, an inverse-kinematics display, gradient/dropout plots, and an ablation table. NeRF images and their table disappear; solver tables move and expand. The original learning curves are retained as Figure 6.

improvement.justification: v1 supported learning applicability mainly through synthetic points and one NeRF scene. v3 substantially strengthens that evidence through object images, real motion-capture inverse kinematics, and real camera-pose evaluation. Appendix F adds meaningful component and robustness investigations, while B.2–B.3.2 fills derivational gaps. These gains outweigh removal of the NeRF example, although absent training-seed uncertainty and insufficiently clear separation of checkpoint selection from testing still limit confidence in performance rankings.
